name: Alcohol withdrawal
summary: Benzodiazepines are first-line. Chlordiazepoxide, diazepam (oral and injectable), clorazepate, and oxazepam carry labeled alcohol-withdrawal indications; lorazepam does not. ASAM (2020) lists carbamazepine and gabapentin as alternatives for mild–moderate withdrawal and phenobarbital for experienced clinicians, usually inpatients. Symptom-triggered dosing (e.g., CIWA-Ar) is common, and thiamine should be given to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.
plainSummary: Stopping heavy drinking suddenly can cause shakiness, sweating, anxiety, seizures, and sometimes a dangerous confusion called delirium tremens. Calming medicines, usually benzodiazepines, keep withdrawal safe while the body adjusts.

approved.indication: Relief of withdrawal symptoms of acute alcoholism (also labeled for anxiety disorders and preoperative apprehension).

population.ages: Adults (not recommended under 6 years; alcohol-withdrawal dosing is for adults)

dosing.target: Repeat as needed until agitation is controlled, then reduce to maintenance levels and taper
dosing.notes: The label notes that parenteral therapy is usually used first, but chlordiazepoxide injection is no longer marketed. Long-acting metabolites accumulate in hepatic impairment and in older adults; consider oxazepam or lorazepam instead. Taper gradually to avoid benzodiazepine withdrawal.

boxedWarnings: Risks from concomitant use with opioids
approved.plainSummary: Chlordiazepoxide is a long-acting calming medicine used for a few days to prevent dangerous alcohol withdrawal, with the dose lowered as symptoms settle.

verified.note: Librium capsules (Bausch ANDA) are listed as marketed in Drugs@FDA; Librium injection is discontinued. The approval year (1960) comes from historical sources.

approved.indication: Treatment of tremor, acute agitation, hallucinosis, and impending delirium tremens or delirium tremens in acute alcohol withdrawal (oral). Injection: symptomatic relief of acute agitation, tremor, impending or acute delirium tremens, and hallucinosis in acute alcohol withdrawal.

dosing.start: Oral: 10 mg three to four times in the first 24 hours. IV/IM: 10 mg initially
dosing.target: Oral: then 5 mg three to four times daily as needed. IV/IM: 5–10 mg in 3–4 hours if necessary
dosing.max: No fixed maximum in the label; some patients need higher doses (increase gradually)
dosing.notes: Long half-life allows self-tapering. Use caution in hepatic impairment, older adults, and respiratory compromise. IV: inject slowly and watch for respiratory depression and hypotension.

boxedWarnings: Risks from concomitant use with opioids
approved.plainSummary: Diazepam is a calming medicine that can be taken by mouth or given by injection to control shaking, agitation, and the risk of delirium during alcohol withdrawal.

verified.note: Valium label (PLR format, rev. 10/2026) and generic diazepam injection label (https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=f466f8a3-f31c-44f4-b0e8-444464f20f66) were both checked. Boxed warnings are from the benzodiazepine class labeling and were not re-read on this label.

approved.indication: Symptomatic relief of acute alcohol withdrawal (also labeled for anxiety and as adjunct for partial seizures).

dosing.start: Day 1: 30 mg, then 30–60 mg in divided doses
dosing.target: Day 2: 45–90 mg; Day 3: 22.5–45 mg; Day 4: 15–30 mg (divided doses); then reduce to 7.5–15 mg/day and stop when stable
dosing.notes: Avoid excessive reductions in total dose on successive days. Converted to desmethyldiazepam, which accumulates in older adults and in hepatic impairment.

boxedWarnings: Risks from concomitant use with opioids
approved.plainSummary: Clorazepate is a long-acting calming pill that can be used on a set, day-by-day lowering schedule to manage alcohol withdrawal.

verified.note: Drugs@FDA shows Tranxene T-Tab 7.5 mg as still listed for prescription; other Tranxene strengths are discontinued. The approval year (1972) comes from historical sources.

approved.indication: Label states: 'Alcoholics with acute tremulousness, inebriation, or with anxiety associated with alcohol withdrawal are responsive to therapy' (within its anxiety indications).

dosing.start: 15–30 mg three or four times daily
dosing.target: 15–30 mg three or four times daily, then taper
dosing.notes: Glucuronidated without active metabolites, so often preferred in hepatic impairment and in older adults. Slower oral absorption makes it less suited to rapid symptom control.

boxedWarnings: Risks from concomitant use with opioids
approved.plainSummary: Oxazepam is a shorter-acting calming pill for alcohol withdrawal that is often chosen for people with liver problems or older adults.

verified.note: Alcohol-withdrawal wording and dosing were confirmed, but the label's phrasing is descriptive rather than a standalone indication. The 120 mg/day maximum is inferred from the labeled 30 mg four-times-daily dosing. Available strengths and the approval year (1965) were not confirmed on this label. The Serax brand is no longer marketed.

approved.indication: Hydroxyzine IM solution is useful in treating 'the acute or chronic alcoholic with anxiety withdrawal symptoms or delirium tremens' when intramuscular administration is indicated.

dosing.target: 50–100 mg IM every 4–6 hours as needed
dosing.notes: IM only; never SC, intra-arterial, or IV. Does not prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens and is not a substitute for benzodiazepines; rarely used for this purpose today. Risks include QT prolongation and anticholinergic effects that can worsen delirium.

approved.plainSummary: A hydroxyzine shot can calm anxiety during alcohol withdrawal, but it does not prevent seizures, so it is used only as an add-on.

source.label: DailyMed: Hydroxyzine hydrochloride injection USP (American Regent)

verified.note: Indication wording, IM dosing, and contraindications were confirmed on the label (rev. 6/2024). Approval year and available strengths were not confirmed. Classified as adjunctive by editorial judgment, since it lacks anticonvulsant protection.

offLabel.use: Alcohol withdrawal, especially with hepatic impairment, in older adults, or when IV/IM dosing is needed
offLabel.notes: Lorazepam is not labeled for alcohol withdrawal but is widely used and accepted by ASAM 2020 as a benzodiazepine option. Its shorter half-life can cause breakthrough symptoms. High-dose IV infusions carry propylene glycol toxicity risk. Benzodiazepine boxed warnings apply.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for anxiety disorders (tablets, extended-release) and, as injection, for status epilepticus and preanesthetic sedation; not labeled for alcohol withdrawal.

dosing.start: 1–2 mg every 4–6 hours (fixed schedule), or 1–4 mg per dose symptom-triggered by CIWA-Ar
dosing.target: Titrate to symptom control, then taper over 3–7 days
dosing.max: No fixed ceiling in monitored settings; avoid prolonged high-dose IV infusions (propylene glycol toxicity)
dosing.notes: Preferred over long-acting benzodiazepines when liver disease or advanced age impairs metabolism. Give thiamine before glucose.

boxedWarnings: Concomitant use with opioids can cause profound sedation, respiratory depression, coma, and death
warnings: Respiratory depression, especially with opioids, alcohol, or other sedatives
Paradoxical agitation and delirium in older adults
Propylene glycol toxicity (lactic acidosis, renal injury) with high IV doses
Concurrent parenteral olanzapine is not recommended
details.plainSummary: A short-acting sedative commonly used to calm the body during alcohol withdrawal, especially in people with liver problems. It is given in a hospital or closely monitored setting and can slow breathing.

references.label: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020), pocket guide
Amato L, et al. Efficacy and safety of pharmacological interventions for the treatment of the alcohol withdrawal syndrome. Cochrane 2011

offLabel.use: Monotherapy or adjunct for moderate–severe or benzodiazepine-resistant alcohol withdrawal (inpatient/ICU)
offLabel.notes: ASAM 2020 limits it to clinicians experienced in its use, mainly in inpatient or monitored settings, because of a narrow therapeutic window and respiratory depression (especially combined with benzodiazepines). Loading-dose protocols vary. Most phenobarbital products are marketed without FDA approval.

details.labeledFor: Phenobarbital tablets and injections are mostly long-marketed unapproved products; labeled historically as a sedative and anticonvulsant. Not labeled for alcohol withdrawal.

dosing.start: Single IV load of about 10 mg/kg ideal body weight over 30 minutes (ED protocols), or 130–260 mg IV/IM; oral taper protocols often start near 60–130 mg every 8 hours
dosing.target: Protocols vary: cumulative IV loading of about 10–30 mg/kg ideal body weight in divided doses over 24 hours in ICU settings; the long half-life (about 80–100 hours) self-tapers
dosing.max: Cumulative loading is usually capped at about 20–30 mg/kg ideal body weight; airway support must be available
dosing.notes: Hold or reduce doses if sedated. Dosing differs by site; follow local protocol.

contraindications: Severe respiratory disease with dyspnea or obstruction
warnings: Respiratory depression, especially with benzodiazepines or opioids
Hypotension with IV use; use in monitored settings only
Habit-forming; paradoxical excitement in older adults
details.plainSummary: A long-acting sedative used in hospitals for severe alcohol withdrawal or when benzodiazepines are not enough. It can slow breathing and affects many other medicines, so close monitoring is needed.

references.label: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020), pocket guide
J Hosp Med summary of ASAM alcohol withdrawal guideline

offLabel.use: Alternative to benzodiazepines for mild–moderate withdrawal (ambulatory), or as an adjunct
offLabel.notes: ASAM 2020 lists it as an appropriate alternative when benzodiazepines are contraindicated or undesirable (e.g., about 600–800 mg/day tapered over 4–9 days). It has not been shown to prevent withdrawal seizures or delirium in severe withdrawal. Cautions: CYP3A4 induction and drug interactions, hyponatremia, blood dyscrasias, SJS/TEN (screen for HLA-B*15:02 in at-risk ancestry), and teratogenicity.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia (Equetro for bipolar I mania); not for alcohol withdrawal.

dosing.start: 200 mg every 6–8 hours (about 600–800 mg/day) on day 1 in ambulatory protocols
dosing.target: Hold near 800 mg/day for 1–2 days, then taper by about 200 mg/day over 4–9 days
dosing.notes: Check sodium, liver tests, and blood counts. Not a substitute for a benzodiazepine in severe withdrawal.

boxedWarnings: Serious dermatologic reactions (SJS/TEN) and the HLA-B*1502 allele
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to carbamazepine or tricyclic compounds
warnings: Strong CYP3A4 inducer (lowers levels of many drugs, including hormonal contraceptives)
details.plainSummary: An anti-seizure medicine that can replace benzodiazepines for mild to moderate alcohol withdrawal in outpatients. It needs blood tests, and it changes the levels of many other medicines.

references.label: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020), pocket guide
Minozzi S, et al. Anticonvulsants for alcohol withdrawal. Cochrane 2010

offLabel.use: Alternative or adjunct for mild–moderate withdrawal, especially when continuing it afterward for AUD
offLabel.notes: ASAM 2020 lists it as an alternative for mild–moderate withdrawal, with regimens such as a 1200 mg load then 600 mg every 6 h, tapering over 4–7 days. It is not adequate alone for severe withdrawal or a history of seizures or delirium tremens. Cautions: sedation, misuse potential, and renal dosing.

details.labeledFor: FDA-approved for postherpetic neuralgia and adjunctive partial-onset seizures; not for alcohol withdrawal.

dosing.start: 1,200 mg load, then 600 mg every 6 hours on day 1 (ASAM example regimen)
dosing.target: About 2,400 mg/day on day 1, then taper over 4–7 days
dosing.max: Up to 3,600 mg/day in studies; reduce for renal impairment
dosing.notes: Not sufficient alone for severe withdrawal or a history of withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens.

warnings: Respiratory depression with opioids or other CNS depressants (FDA 2019 warning)
Misuse and diversion potential (scheduled C-V in some states)
Taper rather than stop abruptly; suicidality warning applies to antiepileptics
details.plainSummary: An anti-seizure and nerve-pain medicine used to ease mild to moderate alcohol withdrawal. It is not strong enough alone for severe withdrawal and can cause drowsiness.

references.label: ASAM Clinical Practice Guideline on Alcohol Withdrawal Management (2020), pocket guide
